title: Who's Calling the Shots? Raising Kids to Love Jesus in a Sports Obsessed World a-sports-obsessed-world
author: Mark Hallock
summary: Pastor and sports dad Mark Hallock addresses Christian parents caught in the escalating demands of youth sports, a culture that asks for more practices, travel, money, and commitment until it becomes the organizing center of family life. He affirms sports as a genuine gift from God but argues they make a terrible god, and he offers four reminders for keeping them in their place. Parents should keep the real end game in view, which is raising children who love and follow Jesus rather than athletes chasing the next level; they should remember that their behaviour in the stands communicates something about Christ; and they should treat sports as discipleship rather than a vehicle for their own unfulfilled dreams. His fourth reminder concerns the local church, asking what family patterns reveal when sports consistently receive the best time and energy. He closes with practical encouragements, including settling priorities before each season, giving permission to say no, being a child's chief encourager, and teaching kids to play for an audience of One.
points: Hallock frames youth sports as a good gift that becomes destructive once it turns into the organizing center of family life.
He argues the goal is not raising great athletes but raising children who love and follow Jesus, which reframes effort, sportsmanship, and improvement as what matters.
Parents are warned against living out their own athletic dreams through their children, making the child's playing time and success the parent's obsession.
He urges families to decide commitments before each season begins, including how they will stay connected to church, and to feel free to say no.
After a hard game, he suggests the most important words may simply be an assurance of love and pride that does not depend on performance.
quotes: They simply get caught up in a sports culture that constantly demands more. More practices. More tournaments. More travel. More money. More commitment. Before you know it, something that began as a wonderful gift has become the organizing center of the entire family.
But we need to remember something important. Our ultimate goal is not to raise great athletes. Our ultimate goal is to raise children who love and follow Jesus.

The way we behave in the stands may teach our children more about following Jesus than what we say on the drive to church. Let's make sure the Jesus we talk about on Sunday is the same Jesus we're seeking to honor on Saturday.

Without even realizing it, we can begin placing those dreams and disappointments on our kids. Their success becomes our success. Their failure feels like our failure. Their playing time becomes our obsession.
This may be the most important reminder of all. Sports are a wonderful gift from God. But they make a terrible god.
The issue isn't that every missed Sunday is sinful. The issue is what our patterns reveal about our priorities.

The truth is this: We don't have to give our children every athletic opportunity to give them a wonderful childhood. In fact, one of the most loving things we can do is teach them that they don't have to do everything.
